Docker Installation Method¶

This method will install the Chavi application using Docker containers.

Prerequisites¶

Docker Desktop:

  • Docker Desktop is a platform for building, shipping, and running applications using containers.

  • It provides a container runtime, a command line interface, and a platform for building and shipping containerized applications.

  • It is available for Windows and macOS.

Please refere to the official Docker documentation for installation instructions:

  • Docker Desktop for Windows

  • Docker Desktop for macOS

After Docker Desktop is installed, you can start the Docker application. Please ensure that proxy settings are configured correctly in the Docker Desktop settings. Without this Docker Desktop will not be able to access the internet.

Installation¶

Create a folder in a location where the CHAVI client application will be installed. Inside this folder, create the following three files:

  • .env

  • docker-compose.yml

  • ngnix.conf

The contents of the files are as follows:

services:
  chaviclient-database:
    image: postgres:17
    restart: always
    container_name: chaviclient-database
    ports:
      - "5433:5432"
    volumes:
      - chaviclient_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    env_file:
      - .env
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  chaviclient-rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:4-management
    restart: always
    container_name: chaviclient-rabbitmq
    ports:
      - "5672:5672"
      - "15672:15672"
    env_file:
      - .env
    volumes:
      - chaviclient_rabbitmq_data:/var/lib/rabbitmq
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "rabbitmqctl status"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 5

  chaviclient-django:
    image: chaviapp/chaviclient:main
    container_name: chaviclient-django
    restart: always
    depends_on:
      chaviclient-database:
        condition: service_healthy
      chaviclient-rabbitmq:
        condition: service_healthy
    env_file:
      - .env      
    volumes:
      - chaviclient_app_data:/app
      - ./media:/app/media
      - ./static:/app/static
      - ./logs:/app/logs
      # DICOM archive (optional — same mount path as the worker; needed for
      # the location write-probe and the "Test location" button. Uncomment
      # together with one of the chaviclient_archive definitions in the
      # top-level volumes: section):
      # - chaviclient_archive:/archive/dicom
    command: ["./entrypoint.docker.sh"]
    # If a remote DICOM node can't be resolved by DNS, pin it here
    # (e.g. a node with only a static IP):
    #extra_hosts:
    #  - "www.dicomserver.co.uk=198.244.176.149"

  # Outbound DICOM Q/R (C-ECHO/C-FIND/C-MOVE/C-GET) originates here.
  # No published ports needed — the container only needs outbound TCP
  # to each remote node's host:port configured in the web UI.
  chaviclient-celery-worker:
    image: chaviapp/chaviclient:main
    container_name: chaviclient-celery-worker
    restart: always
    depends_on:
      chaviclient-database:
        condition: service_healthy
      chaviclient-rabbitmq:
        condition: service_healthy
    env_file:
      - .env
    volumes:
      - chaviclient_app_data:/app
      - ./media:/app/media
      - ./static:/app/static
      - ./logs:/app/logs
      # DICOM archive (optional — uncomment together with one of the
      # chaviclient_archive definitions in the top-level volumes: section):
      # - chaviclient_archive:/archive/dicom
    command: ["celery", "-A", "chavi_client", "worker", "-l", "info", "-Q", "default", "--concurrency=2"]
    # Pin remote DICOM node hostnames to IPs here if container DNS fails:
    #extra_hosts:
    #  - "www.dicomserver.co.uk=198.244.176.149"
    # GPU (optional): uncomment on hosts with an NVIDIA GPU and the
    # nvidia-container-toolkit installed. Lookup-table embedding computation
    # then auto-detects and runs on CUDA; without this block it stays on CPU.
    # deploy:
    #   resources:
    #     reservations:
    #       devices:
    #         - driver: nvidia
    #           count: all
    #           capabilities: [gpu]

  # Deidentification runs on its own queue with a single worker slot so all
  # deid batches are strictly serial across the deployment (see
  # CELERY_TASK_ROUTES in chavi_client/settings.py). Must be upgraded in the
  # same step as the app image: without it, deid tasks publish to the 'deid'
  # queue and are never consumed.
  chaviclient-celery-deid-worker:
    image: chaviapp/chaviclient:main
    container_name: chaviclient-celery-deid-worker
    restart: always
    depends_on:
      chaviclient-database:
        condition: service_healthy
      chaviclient-rabbitmq:
        condition: service_healthy
    env_file:
      - .env
    volumes:
      - chaviclient_app_data:/app
      - ./media:/app/media
      - ./static:/app/static
      - ./logs:/app/logs
      # DICOM archive (optional — same mount path as the other workers;
      # de-archival restore runs in-process inside deid tasks, so this
      # worker needs it too. Uncomment together with one of the
      # chaviclient_archive definitions in the top-level volumes: section):
      # - chaviclient_archive:/archive/dicom
    command: ["celery", "-A", "chavi_client", "worker", "-l", "info", "-Q", "deid", "--concurrency=1"]

  chaviclient-celery-beat:
    image: chaviapp/chaviclient:main
    container_name: chaviclient-celery-beat
    restart: always
    depends_on:
      chaviclient-database:
        condition: service_healthy
      chaviclient-rabbitmq:
        condition: service_healthy
    env_file:
      - .env
    volumes:
      - chaviclient_app_data:/app
      - ./media:/app/media
      - ./logs:/app/logs
    command: ["celery", "-A", "chavi_client", "beat", "-l", "info", "--scheduler", "django_celery_beat.schedulers:DatabaseScheduler"]

  # Inbound DICOM SCP (C-ECHO/C-STORE/C-FIND). The published port must
  # equal the listen port configured at /dicom-server/config/ — remote
  # PACS must reach the Docker host on this port for C-MOVE deliveries.
  chaviclient-dicom:
    image: chaviapp/chaviclient:main
    container_name: chaviclient-dicom
    restart: always
    depends_on:
      chaviclient-database:
        condition: service_healthy
      chaviclient-django:
        condition: service_started
    env_file:
      - .env
    volumes:
      - chaviclient_app_data:/app
      - ./media:/app/media
      - ./logs:/app/logs
    ports:
      - "11112:11112"
    command: ["python", "-m", "dicom_server"]

  chaviclient-proxy:
    image: nginx:latest
    container_name: chaviclient-proxy
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "8001:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
      - ./static:/static:ro
    depends_on:
      - chaviclient-django

volumes:
  chaviclient_postgres_data:
  chaviclient_app_data:
  chaviclient_rabbitmq_data:

  # --- DICOM archive storage (optional) -------------------------------------
  # Uncomment ONE of the two chaviclient_archive definitions below, fill in
  # the parameters (in .env for option A), and uncomment the
  # "- chaviclient_archive:/archive/dicom" line in BOTH the
  # chaviclient-celery-worker and chaviclient-django services (same mount
  # path in both).
  #
  # Option A — network share (SMB/CIFS). Requires NETWORK_USER,
  # NETWORK_DOMAIN, NETWORK_PASSWORD and NETWORK_PATH in .env, e.g.
  # NETWORK_PATH=//nas.example.com/chavi-archive
  # NOTE: uid=0,gid=0 + 0666/0777 is deliberate — this image runs the app as
  # a non-root system user (appuser) whose uid is not pinned, so the share
  # must be world-writable inside the container. Access to the share itself
  # is still protected by the SMB credentials above.
  #
  # chaviclient_archive:
  #   driver_opts:
  #     type: cifs
  #     o: "username=${NETWORK_USER},domain=${NETWORK_DOMAIN},password=${NETWORK_PASSWORD},rw,uid=0,gid=0,file_mode=0666,dir_mode=0777"
  #     device: ${NETWORK_PATH}
  #
  # Option B — a specific local folder instead (on a Windows host with
  # Docker Desktop, e.g. the archive lives on D:\chavi-archive; on Linux use
  # the absolute host path):
  #
  # chaviclient_archive:
  #   driver: local
  #   driver_opts:
  #     o: bind
  #     type: none
  #     device: "D:/chavi-archive"
  #
  # Option C — NFS share on a Linux host (host needs the NFS client:
  # apt-get install nfs-common). Requires NAS_IP and NAS_PATH in .env,
  # e.g. NAS_PATH=/volume1/chavi-archive. "hard" retries I/O forever (data
  # integrity); use "soft" to let archive tasks fail per-study if the NAS
  # drops.
  #
  # chaviclient_archive:
  #   driver: local
  #   driver_opts:
  #     type: nfs
  #     o: addr=${NAS_IP},nfsvers=4.1,hard,noatime
  #     device: ":${NAS_PATH}"

# Sets the max number of simultaneous connections that can be opened by a worker process
events {
   worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
   server {
       include mime.types;
       default_type application/octet-stream;
       sendfile on;
       keepalive_timeout 3600;
       listen 80;
       client_max_body_size 10G; # Add this line to increase the maximum upload size to 1024MB

       # Requests to /static/ are served directly from the /static/ directory
       location /static/ {
           alias /static/;
           expires 7d;
       }

       # Configuration for serving media files
       # location /media/ {
       #     alias /home/app/web/mediafiles/;
       # }

       # Handles all other requests
       location / {
           # Forward requests to Django application
           proxy_pass http://chaviclient-django:8000;

           # Pass important headers to Django for proper request handling
           proxy_set_header Host $host;                          # Original host header
           proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;             # Client's real IP
           proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;  # Chain of IP addresses
           proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;          # Original protocol (http/https)

           # Add timeout settings for long-running requests
           proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
           proxy_connect_timeout 3600s;
           proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
       }
   }
}

SECRET_KEY = your-SECRET_KEY
DJANGO_DEBUG = True
DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS = 127.0.0.1,localhost
DJANGO_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = http://localhost:8001,http://127.0.0.1:8001

# Django DB
DJANGO_DB_ENGINE = django.db.backends.postgresql # Add engine of the database
DJANGO_DB_NAME = chaviclient # Add name of the database
DJANGO_DB_USER = postgres # Add username of the database
DJANGO_DB_PASSWORD = your-password # Add password of the database
DJANGO_DB_HOST = chaviclient-database # Add host of the database
DJANGO_DB_PORT = 5432 # Add port of the database

# Postgres
POSTGRES_USER = postgres
POSTGRES_PASSWORD = your-password
POSTGRES_DB = chaviclient

# Django Superuser
DJANGO_SUPERUSER_USERNAME = admin
DJANGO_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD = admin
DJANGO_SUPERUSER_EMAIL = admin@example.com


# API Settings for Lookup Data
LOOKUP_API_URL=http://backend.chavi.ai/api/v1/lookup/
LOOKUP_API_KEY=secret-api-key-from-chavi-server
LOOKUP_API_TIMEOUT=120
HTTP_PROXY=http://yourproxy:port
HTTPS_PROXY=http://yourproxy:port

# Celery & RabbitMQ
CELERY_BROKER_URL=amqp://chaviuser:chavipassword@chaviclient-rabbitmq:5672/chavi_vhost
RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER=chaviuser
RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS=chavipassword
RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_VHOST=chavi_vhost

# DICOM archive on a network share (only needed for the CIFS/NFS options in
# example_docker-compose.yml; keep this file's permissions at 600 and never
# commit it to version control)
# NETWORK_USER = your-smb-user
# NETWORK_DOMAIN = your-smb-domain
# NETWORK_PASSWORD = your-smb-password
# NETWORK_PATH = //server/share-name
# NAS_IP = 192.168.1.100
# NAS_PATH = /volume1/chavi-archive

After these files have been created you can start editing the .env file. Ensure that the password fields are properly set. If a proxy is used for network access, please ensure that the proxy settings are configured correctly in the .env file.

After the .env file has been edited, you can start the Docker containers by running the following command:

docker-compose up -d

Updating the Software¶

Before any update, please take a backup of the database. To do so please refer to the Database Backup and Restore page.

Stop all running containers in the Docker Desktop application.

After the backup has been taken, you will have to delete the old image and pull the new image.

In Docker desktop, please go to the images section and delete the old image for the CHAVI client. After this is deleted, we would suggest also that you delete the volume created for the chaviclient. However DO NOT delete the volume created for the database.

Once this is done you can pull the new image by running the following command:

docker-compose pull

After the image has been pulled, you can start the containers by running the following command:

docker-compose up -d

Background Task Workers¶

Two Celery workers process background jobs:

  • chaviclient-celery-worker — general tasks (DICOM retrieval, ZIP and clinical data downloads, archive sweeps, scheduled jobs). Runs with two slots (--concurrency=2) on the default queue.

  • chaviclient-celery-deid-worker — deidentification only. Runs with a single slot (--concurrency=1) on the dedicated deid queue, so deidentification batches are processed strictly one after another, even when several patients are de-identified at the same time. This keeps memory and CPU use in check: only one copy of the text-detection models is loaded at a time.

A de-identification job started while another is already running waits in the queue; its task run shows no progress until the running batch finishes. Upgrading the software replaces both workers at once, and any interrupted de-identification run resumes from where it left off.

DICOM Query/Retrieve Networking¶

The chaviclient-dicom container only runs the inbound DICOM service (C-ECHO / C-STORE / C-FIND) on published port 11112. All outbound Query/Retrieve connections to remote DICOM nodes are opened by the chaviclient-celery-worker container (retrieval jobs) and the chaviclient-django container (the C-ECHO test button on the Remote nodes page).

  • Outbound connections need no compose changes — the worker only needs to reach each remote node’s host:port (LAN IP or public hostname).

  • C-MOVE additionally requires the remote PACS to connect back to the Docker host on port 11112 — the host firewall must allow it and the PACS-side destination for our AE title must point at the host IP.

  • C-GET (prefer C-GET on the remote node) receives instances over the same outbound association, so use it when the Docker host is behind NAT or the remote cannot connect back.

  • The published port must match the listen port configured at /dicom-server/config/ and bind_address must remain 0.0.0.0.

See docker_install/README.md in the repository for the full networking table and verification commands.

DICOM Archive Storage (NAS/LAN)¶

If you use the DICOM Archive (see DICOM Archive), remember that the app’s media root inside the containers is /app/media and study folders live at /app/media/processed_dicom/<patient ID>/<study UID>. A location’s path is therefore always a path inside the containers — what it points at on disk depends on how the storage is mounted. Four common setups:

  • Another folder in the app’s media volume — no compose change. Create the location with a relative path, for example dicom_archive; it resolves to /app/media/dicom_archive (host: <compose dir>/media/dicom_archive). Caveat: the archive then lives on the same physical disk as the source data.

  • NAS/LAN share mounted on the Docker host — mount the share on the host first (NFS or SMB, for example at /mnt/nas/chavi-archive — when you put the mount in /etc/fstab, use the _netdev option so the mount waits for the network), then add the bind mount to the volumes: of chaviclient-celery-worker, chaviclient-celery-deid-worker and chaviclient-django:

    volumes:
  - chaviclient_app_data:/app
  - ./media:/app/media
  - /mnt/nas/chavi-archive:/archive/dicom

    Create the location with type Mounted share and path /archive/dicom.

    Warning

    /archive/dicom inside the containers does not need to be created beforehand — the app creates it (with a write probe) when the location is saved, and again at the start of every archive run. But the host side needs a check: if /mnt/nas/chavi-archive does not exist on the Docker host, Docker silently creates it as an empty directory and mounts that — archiving then succeeds, but the data lands on the host disk instead of the NAS. Before starting the containers, confirm the share is really mounted on the host (df -h /mnt/nas/chavi-archive should show the NAS, and on Windows the SMB share must be reachable); after start, docker-compose exec chaviclient-celery-worker ls -ld /archive/dicom should show the share, not an empty fresh directory.

  • Windows host with an SMB share (Docker Desktop) — bind the UNC path directly, no host-side mount needed, again in all three services:

    volumes:
  - //NAS_HOST/chavi-archive:/archive/dicom

    Create the location with type Mounted share and path /archive/dicom.

  • Docker-managed share volume — no host-side mount at all — Docker itself mounts the share as a named volume; the credentials and the share path come from .env. example_docker-compose.yml contains this ready to uncomment. Mount the volume as chaviclient_archive:/archive/dicom in the main worker, the deid worker and the web service (commented lines are included in the example compose), then create the location with type Mounted share and path /archive/dicom.

    SMB/CIFS share (works on Linux hosts and Docker Desktop on Windows):

    volumes:
  chaviclient_archive:
    driver_opts:
      type: cifs
      o: "username=${NETWORK_USER},domain=${NETWORK_DOMAIN},password=${NETWORK_PASSWORD},rw,uid=0,gid=0,file_mode=0666,dir_mode=0777"
      device: ${NETWORK_PATH}        # e.g. //nas.example.com/chavi-archive

    with NETWORK_USER, NETWORK_DOMAIN, NETWORK_PASSWORD and NETWORK_PATH in .env (keep the .env at permissions 600 and never commit it). If the NAS only speaks SMB and the mount fails silently, add vers=3.0 (or vers=2.1) to the o: options and make sure the CIFS client is installed on a Linux host (apt-get install cifs-utils; Docker Desktop on Windows needs nothing extra).

    Hardening variant: instead of putting the username and password in the compose options, keep them in a credentials file on the Docker host — /etc/docker-smb-credentials containing username=, password= and domain=, set to chmod 600 — and use o: "credentials=/etc/docker-smb-credentials,rw,uid=0,gid=0,file_mode=0666,dir_mode=0777".

    NFS share (Linux hosts; the host needs the NFS client — apt-get install nfs-common on Debian/Ubuntu, dnf install nfs-utils on RHEL-based distros):

    volumes:
  chaviclient_archive:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      type: nfs
      o: addr=192.168.1.100,nfsvers=4.1,hard,noatime
      device: ":/volume1/chavi-archive"

    hard (the default) retries I/O forever — data-integrity safe, but a dead NAS will stall archive operations; use soft instead if you would rather have the archive task fail per-study than block, which this application is built to record and recover from. noatime skips access-time updates and is a small performance win for large file copies.

    A specific local folder (e.g. the archive lives on D:\chavi-archive with Docker Desktop on Windows, or a data disk on a Linux host):

    volumes:
  chaviclient_archive:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      o: bind
      type: none
      device: "D:/chavi-archive"

    Note

    uid=0,gid=0 with file_mode=0666,dir_mode=0777 in the CIFS example is deliberate: this image runs the app as a non-root system user (appuser) whose uid is not pinned, so the share must be world-writable inside the container — check yours with docker compose exec chaviclient-django id. Do not use uid=1000,gid=1000 (a common copy-paste) unless the app really runs as uid 1000; with dir_mode=0770 that user would not be able to write the share at all. Access to the share itself remains protected by the SMB/NFS credentials either way, and the only processes in these containers are Django and Celery.

    Caveats of Docker-managed shares:

    • driver_opts are fixed when the volume is created. To change the options, remove the volume first (docker volume rm chaviclient_archive) and start again — only Docker’s mount metadata is removed, the data on the share itself is untouched.

    • If the share is unreachable when the containers start, the volume mount fails and the containers will not start. Start the stack with the NAS up; after a NAS reboot that happened while the stack was running, restart the containers (docker compose down && docker compose up -d) if mounts have gone stale (“Host is down”).

The chaviclient-django (web) container needs the mount too: when a location is saved, the form probes the path for write access in the web container — a path mounted only in the workers fails that validation with “location path is not writable”. The actual archiving runs in chaviclient-celery-worker, while de-archival restore (before de-identification starts, and the per-study safety net during a run) executes inside deidentification tasks on chaviclient-celery-deid-worker — so all three need the mount. chaviclient-celery-beat only dispatches the scheduled sweep and chaviclient-dicom never touches the archive path, so neither of them needs the mount.

Verification after a change:

docker-compose exec chaviclient-celery-worker ls /archive/dicom

then create the mounted location in the UI (it must pass validation) — or better, press the Test location button, which writes a small chavi_archive_write_test.txt you can open on the share to prove the write landed there — then archive one study, and confirm the files under the share:

docker-compose exec chaviclient-celery-worker find /archive/dicom -name '*.dcm' | head

When the “delete local copy after archiving” option is on, the study’s folder under /app/media/processed_dicom disappears after the archive succeeds; de- archiving restores it to the original path.
